1: Encoding and imbalanced classes. Turning words into numbers, and handling rare classes. Lectures twenty one and twenty two and practical twenty one and twenty two.
2: Here is the session map. In the lecture: why encode, types of categories, label and ordinal encoding, one hot encoding, dummy variables, many categories, the concept of target encoding, and the concept of imbalanced classes. In the practical: load the data and count categories, label and ordinal encoding, one hot and dummy variables, frequency and target encoding, find and fix imbalance, and repeat on a second dataset. First we learn each idea, then run it on real Airbnb data.
3: Why encode? A model can only read numbers. A model multiplies values by weights, and it cannot multiply Brooklyn or Private room. The fix is to change every word column into number columns, which is called encoding. In the Airbnb data, room type has three categories, the borough has five, and the neighbourhood has two hundred twenty one. In daily life, a school form stores Class nine B as a code in the computer. Words become numbers, and how we do it changes what the model learns.
4: What types of categories exist? Ask first: does the category have an order? Three kinds. Nominal: no order, like the boroughs Bronx, Brooklyn and so on, or colours red, blue and green. Ordinal: has an order, like shared room less than private room less than entire home, or T shirt sizes small, medium, large. Binary: only two values, like weekend yes or no, or pass or fail. The answer picks the encoding.
5: Label encoding gives one number per category. Bronx is zero, Brooklyn one, Manhattan two, Queens three, Staten Island four. The problem: the numbers look like an order. The model thinks Staten Island, four, is bigger than Manhattan, two, but boroughs have no order. Use it only for tree models and for the target column of a classifier. Label encoding is short, but it invents an order, so avoid it for nominal columns in linear models.
6: Ordinal encoding: you write the order. Shared room is zero with a median price of forty five dollars, private room is one with seventy, and entire home is two with one sixty. Why write it yourself? Alphabetical order would give entire zero and shared two, the wrong way round. When there is a real order, keep it: zero, one, two matches forty five, seventy, one sixty dollars, and the median price goes up with the code.
7: One hot encoding makes one zero or one column per category. Home A in Brooklyn gets a one in the Brooklyn column and zeros elsewhere. Home B in Manhattan gets a one in the Manhattan column. Home C in Queens gets a one in the Queens column. The good news: no false order, and each row has exactly one one. In daily life, it is an attendance sheet with one tick in the right column. One hot is the safe choice for categories with no order.
8: Dummy variables: keep k minus one columns. Why drop one? If a home is not in Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens or Staten Island, it must be in the Bronx, so the Bronx column adds nothing new. Five boroughs means keep four columns, using drop first equals true. The dropped one, the Bronx, is the baseline. Each dummy is read against it: Brooklyn is plus twenty five dollars versus the Bronx's sixty five, Manhattan plus eighty five, Queens plus ten, Staten Island plus ten. Keeping all five columns is called the dummy variable trap.
9: Too many categories? Use one column. Two hundred twenty one areas would make two hundred twenty one one hot columns. Instead, one column with frequency or target encoding. Frequency encoding replaces each area by its share of homes: Williamsburg point zero eight zero, Harlem point zero five four. And for a multi class target, to predict room type with three classes, just number the classes: entire zero, private one, shared two. Many categories become one compact column, and a target with many classes just needs class numbers.
10: Target encoding, the concept: replace a category by its average target. Williamsburg has three thousand one hundred thirty five homes with a median price of one hundred four dollars, so it is encoded as one oh four. Tribeca has one hundred thirty four homes at three hundred dollars. Fort Wadsworth has just one home at eight hundred dollars, but it is encoded as the overall median, one oh five. Two rules. Rule one: use training rows only, or the model peeks at the answers. Rule two: do not trust tiny groups. One eight hundred dollar home cannot speak for a whole area, so with fewer than ten homes, use the overall median. Two hundred twenty one columns become one useful column, if we follow the two rules.
11: Imbalanced classes: when one class is rare, accuracy can fool you. Of the homes, twenty five thousand four hundred seven are entire homes, twenty two thousand three hundred nineteen are private rooms, and only one thousand one fifty eight, two point four percent, are shared rooms, the rare class. The lazy model always says entire home, which is fifty two percent correct, but never finds a shared room. Check the class sizes before you trust accuracy.
12: Four simple fixes for a rare class. One, stratify: keep the same percentage of each class in train and test. Two, class weights: make a mistake on the rare class cost more. Three, resample: copy rare rows or remove some common rows, on training rows only. Four, use the right score: check recall for each class, not just accuracy. Help the model notice the rare class, then measure it fairly.
13: Summary: which encoding when? No order and few categories: one hot with drop first, for example borough becomes four columns. Has an order: your own map, for example room type to zero, one, two. Many categories: frequency or target encoding, for example two hundred twenty one areas become one column. A target with two or more classes: label encoding, room type to zero, one, two. A rare class in the target: stratify, class weights and recall, for example shared rooms at two point four percent. Look at the column type and the number of categories, then pick.
14: The lab, practical twenty one and twenty two, uses two datasets. New York Airbnb twenty nineteen, forty eight thousand eight hundred ninety five homes by sixteen columns, the same file as lectures nineteen and twenty, where we remove eleven homes with price equal to zero. And Online Shoppers, twelve thousand three hundred thirty website visits, a second example with the same code, where only fifteen point six percent of visits buy. The notebook is Lab P twenty one twenty two, encoding and imbalance.
15: Lab step one: load the data and count categories. We read the file, keep only rows with price above zero, and call nunique on the three columns. Room type has three categories, neighbourhood group has five, and neighbourhood has two hundred twenty one. So there are three columns of three sizes: few categories, three and five, and many, two hundred twenty one.
16: Lab step two: label encoding and ordinal encoding. For label encoding, we convert the borough to a category and take its cat codes, which follow the alphabet: Bronx zero, Brooklyn one, Manhattan two, Queens three, Staten Island four. For ordinal encoding, we write our own order as a dictionary, shared room zero, private room one, entire home two, and use map. Now the median price rises with the code, forty five, seventy, one sixty dollars. Cat codes follows the alphabet, while map follows the order we choose.
17: Lab step three: one hot encoding and dummy variables. Get dummies on the neighbourhood group makes one column per borough, and every row sums to one, which we check with sum across axis one. With drop first equals true on both neighbourhood group and room type, we get six dummy columns. The dropped ones, the baselines, are the Bronx and entire home. Drop first removes one column per variable, the baseline.
18: Lab step four: many categories, with frequency and target encoding. For frequency encoding, value counts with normalize gives each neighbourhood's share, and map puts it in a new column: Williamsburg is point zero eight, Harlem point zero five four. For target encoding, we first take an eighty percent training sample, so we do not peek at test rows. Then we group by neighbourhood, take the median price and the count, and use the median only where the count is at least ten, otherwise the overall median. Williamsburg, with three thousand one hundred thirty five homes, gets one oh four dollars. Tribeca, with one hundred thirty four, gets three hundred. Fort Wadsworth, with one home, gets the overall median, one oh five. One column instead of two hundred twenty one.
19: Lab step five: find the imbalance. We count the room types, compute the percentage of each, the ratio of the biggest to the smallest class, and class weights as the length of the data divided by three times the counts. Entire homes are fifty two percent with a weight of point six four. Private rooms are forty five point seven percent with a weight of point seven three. Shared rooms are two point four percent with a weight of fourteen point oh seven. The ratio is twenty one point nine to one. Shared rooms are twenty two times rarer, so each one gets a weight of about fourteen.
20: Lab step six: class weights help the model find the rare class. We split with stratify so each class keeps its share, then train two decision trees of depth five, one plain and one with class weight equals balanced. Look at recall, the percentage of each class found. Without weights, entire homes are found eighty seven point six percent, private rooms seventy nine point eight, and shared rooms only nine point five percent. With balanced weights, entire homes fifty eight percent, private rooms eighty five point eight, and shared rooms sixty five percent. Shared rooms found jump from nine point five to sixty five percent. Accuracy drops from eighty two to seventy three percent, a fair price for not ignoring them.
21: Lab second dataset: Online Shoppers, same code, new data. We read the file, drop duplicates, and one hot encode month and visitor type, which takes the columns from eighteen to twenty seven. The target Revenue is eighty four point four percent no purchase and fifteen point six percent purchase. Buyers found, the recall, is sixty four percent with no weights, and eighty six percent with balanced weights. Same steps, same lesson: class weights find many more of the rare buyers.
22: Key takeaways. One, models need numbers, so encode every word column. Two, no order means one hot, and an order means your own map. Three, keep k minus one dummies, and the dropped one is the baseline. Four, many categories mean frequency or target encoding. Five, for a rare class, stratify, use class weights, and check recall.
